specPoints.text: use the relationship between orbital speed, orbital radius and time period: 2×π × orbital radius orbital speed = time period 2 × π × r v = T

primer.text: One orbit is one lap of a circle, so the distance travelled is the circumference 2πr. Divide that lap by the time taken — the orbital period T — and the orbital speed follows: v = 2πr / T, with r measured from the centre of the orbited body, not its surface.

lessons.title: The orbital speed equation
lessons.opening: A body in circular orbit covers the circumference of a circle, 2πr, in one lap. Average orbital speed divides that distance by the orbital period T: v = 2πr / T, with v in m/s, r the orbital radius in metres, and T the time for one orbit in seconds. The radius always runs from the centre of the orbited body.
keyPoints: In one orbit a body travels the circumference of a circle, 2πr.
The orbital speed equation is v = 2πr / T.
v is the orbital speed in m/s, r the orbital radius in metres, T the orbital period in seconds.
The orbital period is the duration of one full orbit.
The orbital radius runs from the centre of the orbited body to the orbiting object.

low.restatement: Speed = lap distance ÷ lap time = 2πr ÷ T.
low.analogy: A running track: lap length over lap time is your average speed.
low.examPointer: Radius means centre-to-satellite; adding altitude to the body's radius is the classic step students forget.

medium.restatement: The equation is speed = distance/time wearing orbital clothes: distance = 2πr, time = T, radius centre-to-object.
medium.analogy: Clock hands: the tip of the minute hand sweeps 2πr each hour, so its speed is 2πr per 3,600 s.
medium.examPointer: Convert km to m and minutes to seconds before substituting — unit slips cost the answer.

check.stem: State what distance an orbiting body covers in one orbit.
check.modelAnswer: It covers the circumference of the circle, equal to 2πr.

check.stem: Explain why the orbital speed formula divides 2πr by T.
check.modelAnswer: Speed is distance divided by time; in one orbit the distance is the circumference 2πr and the time is the period T, so the average orbital speed must be 2πr divided by T.

lessons.title: Calculating orbital speeds
lessons.opening: Applying v = 2πr / T takes three habits: build the radius from the orbited body's centre (its radius plus any altitude), convert everything to metres and seconds, then substitute. The Hubble Space Telescope, orbiting 560 km up with a 96-minute period above a 6400 km Earth, lands near 7590 m/s.
keyPoints: Orbital radius = radius of the orbited body plus the orbiter's height above its surface.
Convert distances to metres and times to seconds before substituting.

low.restatement: Add altitude to the body's radius, convert to m and s, then substitute.
low.analogy: Measuring a lift's floor count: ground floor (the body's centre) to the top, not just the floors above the roof.
low.examPointer: HST-style questions hide two unit conversions — kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds — before any physics happens.

medium.analogy: A recipe: gather (radius), convert (units), then cook (substitute) — skip a step and the dish fails.
medium.examPointer: Quote the final speed to 3 significant figures — the corpus answer does.

glossary.definition: Average speed around one orbit: v = 2πr / T.
The duration of one full orbit, in seconds.
Distance from the centre of the orbited body to the orbiting object.

workedExample.prompt: A telescope rides 560 km above the Earth's surface and laps the planet every 96 minutes; the Earth's radius is 6400 km. Calculate the orbital speed in m/s.
steps: Orbital radius runs from the Earth's centre: r = 6400 + 560 = 6960 km.
Convert units: r = 6,960,000 m and T = 96 × 60 = 5760 s.
Substitute into v = 2πr / T: v = (2 × π × 6,960,000) / 5760.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The orbital speed is about 7590 m/s (3 s.f.).
